claims.text: The initial materials are multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced by physical or chemical synthesis routes.
The initial nanoparticles have homogeneous elemental distributions with minor local fluctuations.
A minor secondary element can be selected that preferentially occupies nanoparticle surface sites.
Adding this surface-segregating element inhibits diffusion-driven elemental segregation.
Adding this element inhibits segregation associated with atomic-size mismatch.
Preferential surface occupation by the secondary element suppresses differential diffusion.
The surface-segregated secondary element compensates lattice strain.
The surface-segregated secondary element retards diffusion kinetics.
Reduced redistribution and slower diffusion preserve solid-solution phase integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Modified nanoparticles will exhibit smaller compositional gradients than unmodified nanoparticles after identical thermal treatment.
Modified nanoparticles will preserve a single-phase structure better than unmodified nanoparticles.
Unmodified baseline nanoparticles will develop increased surface segregation under the specified thermal conditions.
Unmodified baseline nanoparticles may undergo phase separation or minor phase changes under the specified thermal conditions.
The stabilization effect depends on the identity and concentration of the secondary element.
The proposed effect is specifically relevant to systems having low noble-metal content.
Substantial changes in synthesis conditions or elemental ratios may alter the stabilization effect.
The optimal secondary-element identity and concentration are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in segregation or phase separation relative to an identically treated control would falsify the hypothesis.
